questions.q: What does `stats.norm.ppf(0.05, mu, sigma)` compute, and what is it commonly used for in quant work?
options: The probability density at x=0.05; used for plotting a histogram
The inverse CDF (the value at the 5th percentile) of a fitted normal distribution; commonly used to compute a parametric Value-at-Risk
A random sample drawn from the distribution; used for Monte Carlo simulation
The cumulative probability up to the mean; used for hypothesis testing
questions.explain: ppf is the inverse CDF — given a probability, it returns the value below which that proportion of the distribution falls. At 0.05 on a fitted return distribution, that's the standard way to compute a 1-day 95% parametric VaR.

questions.q: After calling `scipy.optimize.minimize(...)`, what should you always check before trusting the result?
options: result.x, without checking anything else
result.success, to confirm the optimizer actually converged
Nothing — minimize always converges to the global optimum
result.fun must always equal exactly zero
questions.explain: An optimizer can return without having actually converged. The result object's .success field reports whether convergence was achieved, and should be checked before trusting .x or .fun.

questions.q: Why might a Savitzky-Golay filter (`scipy.signal.savgol_filter`) be preferred over a plain moving average when smoothing a noisy price series?
options: It always produces identical output to a moving average, just faster
It fits a local polynomial within each window, which tends to preserve trend shape better than a plain moving average while still reducing noise
It can only be applied to sparse matrices
It removes all NaN values from the series automatically
questions.explain: Savitzky-Golay fits a polynomial of a chosen order within each sliding window, which tends to preserve local curvature and trend shape more faithfully than a simple moving average, while still smoothing out noise.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of `scipy.sparse.csr_matrix` over a dense NumPy array for a matrix that is mostly zeros?
options: It automatically converts all zero values to NaN
It stores only the non-zero entries, saving memory and speeding up supported operations, as long as the matrix stays sparse rather than being densified
It can only store integer values, never floats
It is always faster than a dense array regardless of how many non-zero entries exist
questions.explain: Sparse formats like csr_matrix only store the non-zero entries plus their positions, which saves substantial memory for matrices that are mostly zero — but converting back to a dense array with .toarray() defeats that benefit.

questions.q: According to the lesson's rule of thumb, when should you reach for SciPy instead of plain NumPy?
options: For every single array operation, since SciPy is always faster
Never — SciPy and NumPy are functionally identical

When you need a named algorithm with real complexity behind it (a distribution's CDF, a constrained optimizer, a specific filter, a sparse format), rather than basic array arithmetic NumPy already provides
Only when working with datasets larger than 1 terabyte
questions.explain: Basic array math (arithmetic, broadcasting, simple linear algebra) is already covered by NumPy. SciPy earns its place when you need a well-tested, named algorithm — a distribution, an optimizer, a filter design, or a sparse matrix format — rather than reimplementing one from scratch.
